az802-q-246.objective: Use performance monitoring tools to establish baselines and detect resource bottlenecks affecting server workloads.
keyPoints: Performance Monitor (perfmon) exposes CPU, memory, disk, and network counters for live views and logged collections.
Baselines captured on a healthy server make later deviations meaningful.
PerfMon data complements, not replaces, event-based troubleshooting.
whyOthers: Active Directory Users and Computers manages directory objects and has no performance counters.
Hyper-V Replica replicates VMs to a standby host and does not measure resource usage.
DNS Manager administers zones and records and does not expose system performance counters.

az802-q-247.objective: Configure Data Collector Sets to capture counters, event trace data, and configuration information on a schedule for later analysis.
keyPoints: A Data Collector Set groups performance counters, event trace providers, and configuration data under one schedule.
Logged data can be reviewed as reports, compared against baselines, or imported into analysis tools.
Built-in sets such as System Diagnostics bundle a useful starter collection.
whyOthers: Encryption of volumes is BitLocker or EFS functionality, unrelated to collector sets.
Membership changes are a task for AD tools and delegation, not performance collection.
DHCP scope creation happens in DHCP administration, which has no collector semantics.

az802-q-248.objective: Select processor counters such as % Processor Time when diagnosing CPU saturation, then isolate the consuming process.
keyPoints: Processor % Processor Time shows overall CPU utilization; values persisting near 100% indicate saturation.
Process object counters identify which process consumes the CPU next.
Use context, workload timing, and sustained values rather than single spikes.
whyOthers: Free space measures capacity, not processor demand, and misses CPU saturation entirely.
DNS recursive query counts measure name-service activity, not processor saturation.
DHCP lease counts describe address allocation, not CPU pressure.

az802-q-249.objective: Use Average Disk sec/Read and Average Disk sec/Write to detect storage latency and correlate it with queue depth and workload.
keyPoints: Average Disk sec/Read and sec/Write approximate storage response time in seconds.
Current Queue Length plus latency distinguishes a busy but healthy disk from a saturated one.
Interpret values against the storage type; SSD and NVMe targets tolerate far less latency than spinning disks.
whyOthers: DNS query counts never describe disk response time.
User logon counts measure authentication volume, not storage latency.
DHCP scope utilization tracks address pools, unrelated to disk latency.

az802-q-250.objective: Describe System Insights as local predictive analytics for Windows Server capacity and health signals.
keyPoints: System Insights runs analytics locally on Windows Server 2019+ and forecasts disk, volume, CPU, and networking trends.
Default capabilities raise warnings; administrators can configure thresholds or add custom capabilities.
Data stays on the server, so predictions work without sending telemetry off-box.
whyOthers: DHCP relay is a network forwarding role with no analytics function.
ReFS is a resilient file-system format, not a prediction engine.
System Insights supplements Active Directory rather than replacing any directory service.

az802-q-251.objective: Use the System event log to investigate service, driver, and startup events.
keyPoints: The System log captures events from the operating system and its services, including service control manager errors and driver failures.
Filtering System log events by provider and level shortens diagnosis dramatically.
Retain and clear logs deliberately; deleting them destroys evidence.
whyOthers: Clipboard history is unrelated to service and driver events.
DNS zone files hold resource records, not OS service events.
DHCP lease files record address assignments, not driver failures.

az802-q-252.objective: Use the Application event log to investigate application crashes and application-written events.
keyPoints: Applications and application components write errors and warnings to the Application log.
Crash events frequently name the faulting module, aiding rapid triage.
Pair Application events with reliability and crash dump data for deeper analysis.
whyOthers: The security descriptor database is not an applications log and holds no crash records.
SYSVOL holds policy and scripts for the domain, not application crashes.
DHCP relay logs cover relay delivery only.

az802-q-253.objective: Describe the Security event log as the record of audited security events governed by audit policy.
keyPoints: Security log content is controlled by advanced audit policy, covering logons, object access, policy changes, and directory events.
Absence of events often means no audit subcategory is enabled, not that nothing happened.
Security logs anchor investigations of authentication and access problems.
whyOthers: DNS responses are not audited security events by default.
VM checkpoints live in Hyper-V storage, never in the Security log.
Disk partition layouts are storage configuration, not audited events.

az802-q-254.objective: Configure threshold-based alerting on free-space metrics with appropriate evaluation windows.
keyPoints: Alert rules evaluate a metric or counter against thresholds over a window to reduce false positives.
Local managers can raise warnings too; System Insights provides capacity forecasts with customizable thresholds.
Route alert notifications through the platform so the right team sees them.
whyOthers: Fine-grained password policies govern authentication strength and never alert on disk space.
DFS referrals direct clients to namespace targets and have no alerting behavior.
Conditional forwarders route DNS queries for specific zones, unrelated to capacity thresholds.

az802-q-255.objective: Explain that Azure Monitor data collection rules define which data sources an agent collects and where they go.
keyPoints: A data collection rule (DCR) specifies data sources, transformations where supported, and destinations.
DCRs are associated with specific machines, enabling per-server collection choices.
The Azure Monitor Agent consumes DCR configuration locally.
whyOthers: Storage account keys authorize blob access and define no collection behavior.
Availability sets spread VM instances across fault and update domains, unrelated to collection.
Network security groups filter network traffic and are unrelated to telemetry collection.

az802-q-256.objective: Describe VM Insights as performance and dependency monitoring for supported Azure virtual machines.
keyPoints: VM Insights charts guest performance counters and maps process and dependency topology.
Enabling it deploys the monitoring agents and builds a workspace-backed data pipeline.
Performance views support trends over hours or days to catch slow degradation.
whyOthers: FSMO role management is an AD DS activity, unrelated to guest telemetry.
SMB share configuration is a file-server function, not dependency mapping.
DHCP failover is an address-allocation resiliency feature, not a monitoring tool.

az802-q-257.objective: Correlate CPU counters with process identity, workload context, and duration before acting.
keyPoints: Identify the consuming process, then correlate with workload timing, expected peaks, and duration.
Sustained high CPU with user impact differs from a short scheduled burst.
Compare against a baseline to decide whether the value is abnormal.
whyOthers: Rebooting without collecting data destroys evidence and delays root-cause identification.
Deleting logs removes the records needed to confirm the cause.
Disabling monitoring hides the symptom and guarantees recurrence.

az802-q-258.objective: Test name resolution first when an IP-reachable host cannot be reached by name.
keyPoints: IP success with name failure points to resolver config, hosts entries, suffix search, or DNS records.
Resolve-DnsName reveals which server answered and what record it returned.
Confirm the client is querying the intended DNS server before changing records.
whyOthers: BitLocker protects volumes and has nothing to do with hostname resolution.
VM memory pressure would degrade IP communication too, not just names.
NTFS permissions block resource access after connection, not name lookup.

az802-q-259.objective: Resolve DNS names from PowerShell with Resolve-DnsName as part of name-resolution triage.
keyPoints: Resolve-DnsName queries DNS directly and shows the record type, data, and answering server.
It supports switching servers, cache views, and specific record types for focused checks.
It complements Test-NetConnection, which also reports name resolution plus TCP reachability.
whyOthers: Get-WinEvent reads event logs and does not resolve names.
Get-Volume reports volume health and space, unrelated to DNS.
Test-ComputerSecureChannel validates machine-account trust, not DNS resolution.

az802-q-260.objective: Explain that Kerberos authentication tolerates limited clock skew, so significant time drift breaks domain logon.
keyPoints: Kerberos tickets are stamped with time and rejected beyond the policy skew threshold (default five minutes).
Clock problems typically appear as pre-authentication failures and intermittent authentication errors.
Verify time service health before changing authentication settings.
whyOthers: NTFS permissions are evaluated against security tokens, not time zones.
DHCP serving is independent of Kerberos skew tolerance.
VHDX files remain writable regardless of clock drift.

az802-q-261.objective: Identify W32Time as the Windows service responsible for time synchronization.
keyPoints: W32Time synchronizes clocks from domain or manual sources using NTP.
Domain members chain from the PDC Emulator hierarchy by default.
Stopping or misconfiguring W32Time is a common cause of authentication drift.
whyOthers: DFS Replication synchronizes SYSVOL and replicated folders, not clocks.
The Server service hosts shares, unrelated to time.
The Workstation service handles redirector duties and does not manage time sources.

az802-q-262.objective: Recognize the forest-root PDC Emulator as the authoritative time source for the domain hierarchy.
keyPoints: The forest-root PDC Emulator is the top of the domain time hierarchy and should synchronize from reliable external NTP.
Other DCs and members derive time from the hierarchy beneath it.
Configuring authoritative time sources is a deliberate, documented step.
whyOthers: DHCP servers lease addresses and are not time authorities.
Disk size has no role in time hierarchy placement.
Member servers sync from the hierarchy; promoting an arbitrary one breaks the chain.

az802-q-263.objective: Review update error codes, Windows Update logs, service state, disk space, and connectivity when updates fail repeatedly.
keyPoints: Modern update logging uses ETL traces; Get-WindowsUpdateLog converts them into a readable WindowsUpdate.log.
Error codes plus service state separate service failures from payload, cache, and network causes.
Disk space and connectivity failures routinely masquerade as update errors.
whyOthers: Checkpoint age is a Hyper-V concern, not an update-service diagnostic.
Schema ownership affects directory changes only, not update servicing.
Namespace targets govern referrals and do not explain update failures.

az802-q-264.objective: Recover a failed boot after a driver change with Safe Mode or a recovery environment before destructive options.
keyPoints: Safe Mode and Windows RE let you remove or roll back the offending driver while preserving data.
Boot-recovery actions should target the most recent change first.
Confirm backups before aggressive recovery steps.
whyOthers: Deleting the AD database is destructive and unrelated to a driver boot failure.
Zone type is a DNS design choice, irrelevant to boot configuration.
DHCP scopes govern address allocation, nothing about booting.

az802-q-265.objective: Inspect and modify Boot Configuration Data with BCDEdit from recovery environments.
keyPoints: BCDEdit views and edits boot configuration entries, including safe-mode and recovery settings.
Always export the BCD store before edits so you can restore it.
Wrong BCD edits can make a system unbootable; verify each change carefully.
whyOthers: nslookup resolves DNS names and never touches boot data.
dfsutil manages namespaces and roots, unrelated to boot entries.
DHCP scope cmdlets configure address pools, not boot configuration.

az802-q-266.objective: Correlate guest disk latency, host storage latency, queue depth, and VM storage configuration after a storage migration.
keyPoints: Combine guest-visible latency counters with host-level storage counters to locate the bottleneck.
Queue depth reflects outstanding I/O and helps separate latency pressure from workload bursts.
Review VM storage configuration (VHDX placement, cache, per-host paths) after any migration.
whyOthers: Password length is irrelevant to I/O performance.
AD site names describe replication topology, not storage latency.
DNS TTL controls record caching, unrelated to VM storage.

az802-q-267.objective: Investigate a stopped service using service configuration, dependencies, startup type, and System event log evidence.
keyPoints: Startup type, dependencies, and logon account all determine whether a service starts.
System log events record failure, delay, and dependency reasons.
Differentiate intentional configuration, delayed start, and failure causes.
whyOthers: Desktop wallpaper is cosmetic and carries no diagnostics.
DNSSEC chain health does not stop local services.
DHCP reservations never affect service startup.

az802-q-268.objective: Query recent Windows events with Get-WinEvent, including filtered queries across logs.
keyPoints: Get-WinEvent supports log paths, provider filters, severity filters, and scripted repeat queries.
FilterHashtable queries are efficient and reproducible for investigation.
It complements Event Viewer for exploratory review of logs.
whyOthers: Get-ADReplicationSite manages replication-site objects, not event logs.
Get-Volume reports storage health, not log events.
Get-VMSwitch manages Hyper-V virtual switch objects; it never reads events.

az802-q-269.objective: Use repadmin as the first tool for detailed AD replication partner status.
keyPoints: repadmin /replsummary and /showrepl reveal partner state, error codes, and last-success times.
Error codes and invocation IDs map to specific known remedies.
Confirm DNS and RPC connectivity before deeper replication repairs.
whyOthers: robocopy copies files and folders, not directory replication metadata.
diskpart manages disks and partitions, unrelated to AD replication.
mstsc starts Remote Desktop sessions, not replication diagnostics.

az802-q-270.objective: Recognize DNS, RPC/firewall, time, and topology problems as common causes of AD replication failures.
keyPoints: DC discovery failures via DNS commonly surface as replication failures.
Blocked RPC traffic, excessive clock skew, and broken site-link design all contribute.
repadmin and Directory Service log events localize causes.
whyOthers: A full printer queue is a local spooler issue, unrelated to replication.
Screen savers have no network role in replication.
Desktop shortcuts are shell items, not replication factors.

az802-q-271.objective: Check DFSR state, event logs, and initial synchronization when SYSVOL is not shared.
keyPoints: SYSVOL availability depends on DFSR reaching a healthy, initialized state on each DC.
DFSR events and diagnostics reveal membership, initial sync, and error states.
Do not rebuild SYSVOL without understanding member state first.
whyOthers: The public DNS root has no bearing on local SYSVOL shares.
DHCP reservations for printers are unrelated to SYSVOL.
VM display adapters do not control folder sharing.

az802-q-272.objective: Check DNS, time, secure channel, and domain-controller reachability when local logon works but domain logon fails.
keyPoints: Domain logon needs DC discovery (DNS), time tolerance, a valid machine-account trust, and network path.
Test-ComputerSecureChannel and nltest quickly expose trust problems.
Local logon success narrows the issue to domain dependencies, not credentials alone.
whyOthers: Deduplication governs file storage, unrelated to authentication.
GPU partitioning is a virtualization feature, not a logon factor.
FSRM file screens regulate file types, not logon ability.

az802-q-273.objective: Evaluate effective share and NTFS permissions against the user's security-token groups when access is denied to a share.
keyPoints: Access requires passing both the share layer and NTFS for the groups in the user's token, including deny entries.
Effective access tools compute the intersection instead of manual guessing.
Group membership and deny ACEs often explain surprising denials.
whyOthers: DNS TTL affects record lifetime only.
CPU frequency has nothing to do with file authorization.
DHCP lease age never modifies access checks.

az802-q-274.objective: Check disk signature conflicts, SAN policy, and shared-bus safety before bringing an offline disk online.
keyPoints: Presented disks can arrive offline due to signature collision, SAN policy, or read-only status.
Bringing the wrong disk online can corrupt data, especially on shared or replicated LUNs.
Confirm disk identity uniqueness before online and format decisions.
whyOthers: DNS scavenging cleans stale records, not offline disks.
Hyper-V Replica test mode provisions its own copies and never touches host disks.
Password policy has no effect on disk state.

az802-q-275.objective: Use chkdsk to check file-system metadata and, with appropriate flags, scan for bad sectors.
keyPoints: chkdsk validates file-system metadata and can repair certain logical errors.
With /r it scans for bad sectors, which on large volumes takes significant time.
Run chkdsk deliberately on production volumes and schedule around operations.
whyOthers: DHCP lease replication is not a file-system concept.
DNS recursion is a resolver behavior, not disk maintenance.
Trust direction is an AD concept, unrelated to chkdsk.

az802-q-276.objective: Follow supported resiliency repair steps (health review, disk replacement, rebuild) for degraded Storage Spaces virtual disks.
keyPoints: Get-PhysicalDisk, Get-VirtualDisk, and health status identify which physical disk degraded the space.
Replace failed media and allow resiliency to rebuild rather than deleting the pool.
Verify rebuild completion and healthy status after replacement.
whyOthers: Deleting the pool destroys all virtual disks on it, a catastrophic shortcut.
Formatting every disk erases data needlessly and does not address the failure.
Disabling monitoring removes the tooling that detects degradation.

az802-q-277.objective: Compare OS support, agent version, permissions, connectivity, and extension logs when an Arc extension fails on one server.
keyPoints: Host-specific failures usually mean a prerequisite, version, identity, or connectivity difference.
Extension logs and Connected Machine agent state localize extension and platform causes.
Verify endpoint and proxy connectivity for the affected server.
whyOthers: Desktop themes are client-shell cosmetics, unrelated to extension success.
AD group scope alone would not explain a server-local failure pattern.
DNS TTL does not change extension download or install behavior.

az802-q-278.objective: Capture evidence and change one variable at a time to preserve causality during troubleshooting.
keyPoints: Evidence-first workflows keep logs intact and maintain reproducibility.
One variable at a time makes cause and effect separable.
Document each change so rollback remains possible.
whyOthers: Deleting logs destroys the evidence trail needed for diagnosis.
Bundled changes confuse cause with effect and cannot be reproduced.
Reboot loops waste time and can worsen the problem.

az802-q-279.objective: Frame intermittent failures around timestamps, affected scope, recurrence pattern, and correlated logs.
keyPoints: Intermittent problems need correlation across time, systems, and dependencies.
Establish affected scope and recurrence before hunting root cause.
Use event timestamps and monitoring to anchor the failure window.
whyOthers: Rebuilding a forest is a catastrophic last-resort recovery, not an opening move.
Assigning blame by machine age ignores evidence and wastes effort.
Disabling security controls to simplify testing creates a second, worse problem.

az802-q-280.objective: Judge alerts by threshold duration, recurrence, workload impact, and corroboration, not by a lone incident.
keyPoints: Alert quality is a design property: which threshold, over which window, with which recurrence.
Short-lived single incidents may reflect transient spikes; corroborate before acting.
Tune thresholds with operational data to balance noise and missed events.
whyOthers: The alert name alone never carries enough context to decide.
Computer-account passwords are authentication state, unrelated to alert triage.
DNS zone serials track zone changes, not alert validity.
